The Gangetic hairfin anchovy Setipinna phasa exhibits a relatively rapid early life history, with hatching occurring just six days [ab = six days] after fertilisation at a stable water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, termed prolarvae at this stage, are minuscule, with an estimated wet weight at birth of just 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly one millimetre typical of many engraulid species. This lecithotrophic phase is brief, and the onset of first exogenous feeding follows quickly as the yolk reserves are depleted. The timing of these early events is strongly modulated by ambient thermal conditions; at the reference temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the developmental pace is moderately rapid, allowing the prolarvae to transition to actively feeding, free-swimming larvae within a few days post-eclosion. This abbreviated larval period is likely an adaptation to the highly productive, turbid estuarine environments of the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta where this species is predominantly found, favouring a rapid shift to planktivory.

As individuals progress through the larval and juvenile stages, their growth trajectory becomes strongly determinate. The species attains a maximum recorded standard length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], which represents the ultimate size ceiling for Setipinna phasa. This asymptotic length is a key metric of its life-history strategy, situating S. phasa as a moderately sized anchovy within its genus. Corresponding to this ultimate length, the maximum wet weight achieved by fully grown adults has been documented at 372 grams [Wwi = 372 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions that conform closely to the general fusiform body plan of the species. Field surveys indicate that this ultimate size is typically reached after several years of growth, with a noticeable deceleration in the annual increment once individuals surpass approximately thirty centimeters. Comparative data from congeners suggest that this determinate growth pattern is typical of short-lived, multiple-spawning clupeiform fishes inhabiting seasonal tropical rivers.

The onset of sexual maturation in Setipinna phasa occurs at a considerably smaller size than the ultimate maximum. Specifically, puberty is reached at a standard length of 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters], at which point the gonads begin active gametogenesis. The wet weight at this pubertal stage is approximately 37.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 37.2 grams], representing less than ten percent of the ultimate body mass. This early maturation relative to final size is a classic feature of an opportunistic or periodic life-history strategy, allowing individuals to contribute to the breeding population within their first or second year of life. The relatively modest size at first maturity likely reflects the selective pressures of a variable and often food-limited riverine environment, where delaying reproduction to achieve a larger adult size carries a substantial risk of pre-reproductive mortality. Histological examinations of the ovaries confirm that vitellogenesis is well underway by the time females reach this pubertal length.

Reproductive output in this anchovy is substantial, though it is distributed across numerous spawning events within a single season. Females produce between approximately 65 and 66 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 65 and 66 eggs per spawning event], and this spawning activity is repeated nearly every day during the peak breeding season [F_R_i = spawning activity is repeated nearly every day during the peak breeding season]. Consequently, the annual spawning frequency is very high, with individuals capable of spawning daily for extended periods, given suitable environmental cues and food availability. This iteroparous, batch-spawning strategy is a hallmark of clupeiform fishes, maximising lifetime fecundity in a system where larval survival is highly stochastic. The combination of a moderate clutch size with an extremely high spawning frequency results in a very high maximum reproductive rate. Notably, this high fecundity is sustained under optimal thermal conditions at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a temperature that represents the typical late spring and early summer water temperatures in their native habitat when spawning intensity peaks.

Despite its high reproductive potential, the Gangetic hairfin anchovy is not particularly long-lived. This lifespan, while typical for a fish of its size, is relatively short in an absolute sense and is achieved primarily under stable environmental conditions at the reference temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. In practice, few individuals likely attain this maximum longevity due to intense fishing pressure and natural predation pressures throughout their range. The species demonstrates a clear trade-off between early and high reproductive investment and a short overall lifespan. This combination of rapid early growth, early puberty at 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters] standard length, and a moderate maximum longevity of nine years [am = nine years] define at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]s S. phasa as a classic example of a periodic strategist adapted to the predictable seasonal flooding cycles of the Ganges-Brahmaputra basin, balancing high fecundity with a compressed adult life stage.
